wrong: Witness who is the opposing party in the case
That is an adverse party witness. A hostile witness is your own witness who turns out antagonistic or evasive.
Witness whose testimony rests on special knowledge
That is an expert witness.
Witness who testifies only to the accused's reputation
That is a character witness.
Act/Omission, Damage to another, Proof of motive
Damage and motive are not elements. A felony is an act or omission punishable by the RPC, done by deceit (dolo) or fault (culpa).
Intent, Overt act, Consummation of the crime
Felonies include attempted and frustrated stages and acts by culpa, so intent and consummation are not required elements.
Act/Omission, Punishable by special law, Malice
Acts punished by special laws are offenses, not felonies. Felonies are punished by the Revised Penal Code (Art. 3).

wrong: Some acts done but stopped by outside causes
That is the attempted stage: not all acts of execution were performed.
All acts done and the felony accomplished
That is the consummated stage.
Acts done that can never produce the felony
That is an impossible crime (Art. 4(2)).
Murder and rebellion punished separately
Under the Hernandez doctrine, killings in furtherance of rebellion are absorbed, not punished separately.
Rebellion absorbed in murder
Reversed: the murder is absorbed in the rebellion, not the other way round.
Complex crime with the graver penalty
There is no complex crime of rebellion with murder; common crimes done in furtherance of rebellion are absorbed (People v. Hernandez).
One fixed term set by the court
That is a straight penalty. The Indeterminate Sentence Law requires a minimum and a maximum.
Suspension of sentence for first offenders
That is probation (PD 968).
Deduction of time for good conduct
That is good conduct time allowance.
Maximum is twice the most severe penalty
The limit is three times, not twice, the most severe penalty, and never more than 40 years (Art. 70).
All penalties served at the same time
Simultaneous service applies only where the nature of the penalties allows it; the three-fold rule limits successive service.
Maximum 30 years for any number of crimes
The cap under Art. 70 is 40 years, not 30.
Act is lawful so there is no crime
That describes a justifying circumstance. With an absolutory cause the act is still wrong, but no penalty is imposed.
Penalty is lowered by one degree
That is the effect of a privileged mitigating circumstance.
Penalty is raised to the maximum
That is the effect of an aggravating circumstance.
Act stopped by outside causes before completion
That is an attempted felony.
Act completed but its result did not happen
That is a frustrated felony.
Act committed by a person exempt from liability
That involves an exempting circumstance, not an impossible crime.
Conspiracy proven only by a written agreement
Conspiracy need not be written. Implied conspiracy is shown by the coordinated acts of the accused.
Conspiracy proven by a prior express agreement
That is express conspiracy; implied conspiracy is inferred without proof of a prior agreement.
Proposal to commit a felony to another person
That is proposal (Art. 8), not implied conspiracy.
Each crime punished with its own penalty
That is the rule for separate crimes, the opposite of absorption.
Single act producing two grave felonies
That is a compound crime (Art. 48), punished with the penalty for the most serious crime.
Graver penalty imposed in its maximum period
That is the penalty rule for complex crimes, not absorption.
Difference between two witnesses' accounts
That is an inconsistency in testimony, not variance.
Difference between trial and appeal rulings
That is a reversal or modification on appeal, not variance.
Change of the charge before arraignment
That is amendment of the information (Rule 110, Sec. 14).
Prision mayor if death results
Under RA 11053 (2018), the penalty when death results is reclusion perpetua, not prision mayor.
Reclusion temporal if death results
Under RA 11053 (2018), the penalty when death results is reclusion perpetua, not reclusion temporal.
Death penalty if death results
The death penalty was abolished by RA 9346 (2006); RA 11053 imposes reclusion perpetua.
Cause that makes the act lawful
That is a justifying circumstance. With an absolutory cause the act remains a crime, but the offender is not punished.
Cause that lowers the penalty by degrees
That is a privileged mitigating circumstance.
Cause that raises the penalty to its maximum
That is an aggravating circumstance.
Entrapment is absolutory, instigation is not
Reversed: instigation induces the crime and is absolutory; entrapment only catches an offender who was already willing.
Both are absolutory causes for the accused
Only instigation is absolutory.
Both are aggravating against the accused
Neither is aggravating. Entrapment is allowed, while instigation frees the accused.
Doubt resolved in favor of prosecution
Reversed: under pro reo, doubts in penal laws are resolved in favor of the accused.
Law applied exactly as written always
That is literal interpretation, not the pro reo principle.
Penal laws applied retroactively always
Penal laws apply retroactively only when favorable to the accused (Art. 22); not always.
Mistake in the blow
That is aberratio ictus.
Mistake in identity
That is error in personae.
Act without any intent
Felonies by culpa have no intent at all. Praeter intentionem means the result went beyond what was intended.
Second conviction under the same title of the Code
That is recidivism (Art. 14(9)).
Third conviction for theft within ten years
That is habitual delinquency (Art. 62).
Committing a felony while out on bail
Being on bail is not serving a sentence. Quasi-recidivism needs a final conviction, then a new felony before or while serving it.
Overt acts begun but not all acts of execution performed
That is the attempted stage.
All acts done and every element of the felony accomplished
That is the consummated stage.
Acts that can never produce the crime because of impossibility
That is an impossible crime.
All acts of execution done but the result did not follow
That is the frustrated stage.
Preparatory acts done but no overt act begun yet
Preparatory acts are generally not punishable; the attempted stage begins with overt acts.
Acts done that could never produce the felony
That is an impossible crime.
Homicide and robbery punished separately
Robbery with homicide is a special complex crime with a single penalty.
Robbery absorbed as a mere aggravating factor
Robbery is not reduced to an aggravating circumstance; both are joined into one special complex crime.
Graver penalty applied in its maximum period
That is the rule for ordinary complex crimes under Art. 48.
Accumulating ill-gotten wealth of at least P75 million
RA 7080 first set P75 million, but RA 7659 lowered the threshold to P50 million.
Taking public funds of any amount for personal use
That describes malversation (Art. 217), which has no minimum amount.
Receiving gifts in exchange for official favors
That is bribery (Arts. 210-211), not plunder.
Circumstances that lower the penalty
Those are mitigating circumstances.
Circumstances that free the accused
Those are exempting circumstances.
Circumstances that make the killing lawful
Those are justifying circumstances.
Rising publicly in arms to remove allegiance
That is rebellion (Art. 134).
Seizing power suddenly by persons in authority
That is coup d'etat (Art. 134-A).
Inciting others to rebel through speeches
That is inciting to rebellion (Art. 138).
Public uprising to prevent a law's execution
That is one objective of sedition (Art. 139), not rebellion.
Swift attack on military installations by officers
That is coup d'etat (Art. 134-A).
Levying war on behalf of a foreign enemy
That is treason, which requires allegiance to the Philippines and a foreign enemy.
Armed uprising to overthrow the government
That is rebellion.
Revealing defense secrets to a foreign power
That is espionage (Art. 117 and Commonwealth Act 616).
Inciting others to war against the state
That is not treason; treason requires levying war or adhering to the enemy, giving aid or comfort.
Right to bail before conviction for any offense
Bail is a separate constitutional right, and not for every offense; it is not the Miranda doctrine.
Right to confront witnesses during the trial
That is the right of confrontation.
Right to a speedy trial after the arraignment
That is the right to a speedy trial.
Evidence seized with a valid warrant is always admissible
Not the doctrine. The fruit of the poisonous tree concerns evidence derived from an illegal search or seizure.
Confessions taken without counsel may still be used later
The opposite: such confessions are inadmissible (1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 12).
Evidence found by private persons is always inadmissible
Wrong: the exclusionary rule binds the State, not private persons (People v. Marti).
Mental age below 2 years
That is idiocy, a more severe level.
Mental age of 7-12 years
That is moronity (feeblemindedness), which is not an exempting circumstance.
Mental age of 12-15 years
A mental age above 7 is not imbecility and is not exempting.
Unlawful aggression, Reasonable necessity, Relationship to victim
Relationship matters in defense of relatives, not in self-defense.
Imminent danger, Equal weapons, Lack of provocation
Equal weapons are not required; the means need only be reasonably necessary.
Unlawful aggression, Actual injury, Lack of provocation
The defender need not be injured first; the second element is reasonable necessity of the means.
Evidence obtained by private individuals is inadmissible
Reversed: Marti held that the Bill of Rights binds the State, so evidence found by private persons is admissible.
Warrantless searches by police are always valid
Marti did not hold that; the case concerned a search by a private forwarding company.
Evidence from courier inspections needs a warrant
The courier's own inspection in Marti needed no warrant because it was a private act.
